newsitem.title: UK: Bruton senses historic breakthrough for N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Bruton senses historic breakthrough for N.Ireland.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Wednesday an historic breakthrough is possible for peace in Northern Ireland and urged the IRA to deliver on its long-promised ceasefire.

In a speech to the Oxford Union, Bruton said a detailed plan for peace was already in place. The first element consisted of peace talks open to all political parties and involving both the British and Irish governments, and the second was an end to Irish Republican Army violence.

"The Republican Movement should make up its mind, once and for all, unreservedly to enter the political process, and throw away for good the crutch of violence or threatened violence. Once it does that, the road to peace and prosperity is open to all," he said.

Bruton was to meet Britain's new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair on Thursday. Political analysts hoped Blair's landslide election victory would enable him to make better progress towards a lasting peace in the British-ruled province.
"I come with a sense that an historic breakthrough is possible in Northern Ireland," Bruton said.
He outlined achievements of the peace talks that opened in Belfast nearly a year ago and which will resume on June 3.

Britain and Ireland have set up an international group to deal with decommissioning of arms, lifted broadcasting restrictions on Sinn Fein, the political arm of the IRA, paved the way for a release of 36 IRA prisoners and the transfer of others from British to Irish jails, and set up the talks process.
"Everything is now in place to end the agony of Northern Ireland. If we fail to move forward towards a settlement, the excuses for inertia on one side or the other will gain credence," said Bruton.

The IRA, which has fought for more than 25 years to oust Britain from Northern Ireland, ended its 17-month ceasefire in 1996 accusing then-prime minister John Major of intransigence and striking deals with the pro-British Ulster Unionists to stay in power.
With a 179-seat majority in the new parliament, Blair will not face a similar stranglehold but he has insisted that the IRA call a new truce before entering all-party talks.

"If they (the Republican movement) make good their promise to take the political road, the two governments will receive them...into inclusive talks where no topic is excluded and all the relevant players are present," Bruton promised.
But he warned that "the Irish and British democracies will not be the hostages of the Republican movement. We want peace, but we will not compromise our democratic values."
Turning his attention to the Unionists, Bruton said their traditions have equal validity and they have nothing to fear from talks, once the threat of violence is off the table.

"Let us focus on the real issue, which is the content and quality of a comprehensive accommodation between the two communities, the two allegiances, which share the same lands and streets, and will always do so," he said.
Bruton urged the parties in Northern Ireland to grasp an opportunity, which he said is "unparalleled in our history to put behind us the troubles of centuries." REUTER PAR
